cases.learnTitle: Contrast-enhanced chest CT: the four chambers and the great vessels
cases.contextSource: Dataset table (age, sex, scanner); no clinical history is distributed.
cases.referenceSummary: 13 structure outlines come from the dataset's own segmentation (heart, aorta, pulmonary veins, venae cavae, left atrial appendage and the arch branches that lie in the cropped chest): model-assisted and verified by radiologists, not drawn from scratch and not re-reviewed here. 6 further outlines (heart chambers, left ventricular muscle, pulmonary arteries) are unreviewed AI drafts that pass automatic checks; they are never graded. The aorta measures about 183 HU at the heart's levels, so this scan was enhanced with intravenous contrast (the inferior vena cava, 127 HU, is less dense: an early phase). Scanner: philips iqon - spectral ct, 120 kV.
cases.learnNotes: On an axial chest CT the great vessels keep the same order from patient right to left and front to back, so name them by where they sit rather than by how bright they are. The ascending aorta is the round vessel in the middle of the heart's upper part; the descending aorta is the round vessel in front of the spine on the left. The superior vena cava lies to the right of the ascending aorta and drains into the right atrium; the inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below, next to the liver. The four pulmonary veins run from the lungs into the back of the left atrium, and the small ear-shaped left atrial appendage sits beside the pulmonary trunk on the left. After an injection of contrast the arteries are brightest in the arterial phase; veins and the right heart fill later, so a vein can be dark on the same slice as a bright aorta (Learning Radiology, Ch. 3). Four chambers on an axial slice at the level of the ventricles: the right ventricle is the most anterior chamber, directly behind the sternum; the right atrium forms the right border of the heart; the left atrium is the most posterior chamber, in front of the esophagus and descending aorta, with the pulmonary veins entering its back corners; the left ventricle lies to the left, with the thickest wall. The interventricular septum separates the ventricles. The aortic root sits in the middle, between the chambers. With contrast, the blood is bright and the muscle grey; without it, blood and muscle are almost the same density and the chambers cannot be told apart (Learning Radiology, Ch. 3). Look at the blood inside the aorta and the heart. Unenhanced blood is about as dense as soft tissue (roughly 30 to 50 HU, similar to muscle). After an intravenous injection the aorta fills first and is often 250 HU or more in the arterial phase, while the veins and the right heart stay darker; later (the venous phase) the veins are brighter and the aorta is dimmer. Contrast is what lets you see the chambers, the vessel walls and filling defects; an unenhanced CT is still useful for calcium, the size of the heart and the aorta, and fat (Learning Radiology, Ch. 13).
